client: I've been really struggling lately with how much is piling up at work. My boss just dumped two new projects on me with these insane deadlines, and I'm already stretched thin at the marketing agency. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the workload is still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a real weight right now, and that skepticism about whether talking will help makes a lot of sense when the pressure feels so concrete and immediate. You're right that our conversation won't erase the deadlines — but what we *can* explore is how your thoughts about the situation might be adding to the burden, which could actually change how you experience and navigate it. I'm curious, when you imagine facing those two new projects, what's the very first thought that comes to mind?

client: The first thought that comes to mind is honestly just "I'm going to fail." Like, I can already picture myself dropping the ball on one of them, missing a deadline, and my boss losing all confidence in me. It's this immediate dread, almost like the outcome is already decided before I've even started.
therapist: That thought — "I'm going to fail" — sounds like it arrives so fast and feels so certain, almost like your mind is presenting it as fact rather than a fear. This is something we call fortune-telling in CBT, where our brain jumps to a painful outcome before any evidence is in. What actual evidence do you have from your past experience at work that might challenge or complicate that prediction?

client: I mean, I guess I've pulled through tight deadlines before — there was that big campaign launch last spring where everything felt impossible and we actually delivered it on time. But it feels different now, like that was a fluke or I just got lucky, and this time the stakes are higher so I won't be able to pull it off again. I don't know, it's hard to let that past success actually count for anything in my head.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can actually recall that campaign success — your mind just has a habit of labeling it "luck" to keep it from counting as real evidence of your capability. That pattern, dismissing your own wins as flukes while treating feared failures as certainties, is worth gently challenging. What do you think would need to be true for that spring campaign success to count as *genuine skill* rather than luck?

client: I guess if it happened more than once, maybe I'd believe it was skill and not just luck. But even as I say that, I realize I've actually hit deadlines consistently over the past two years, and my brain is still finding ways to dismiss it. It's frustrating because I can see the logic of what you're saying, but emotionally it just doesn't land the same way — like I know it intellectually but I can't make myself feel it.
therapist: That gap between knowing something intellectually and actually *feeling* it is one of the most frustrating parts of this work, and you're not alone in experiencing it — it's incredibly common and doesn't mean the logic is wrong, just that the emotional brain needs more than one conversation to catch up. What you just did, though — noticing your brain dismissing a *pattern* of two years of consistent success — is actually a really important moment of self-awareness. I'm wondering, if a close colleague described their own track record the way you just described yours, what would you genuinely feel about their abilities?

client: Honestly, if a colleague told me they'd been hitting deadlines consistently for two years I'd think they were pretty competent and reliable, I wouldn't even question it. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself it just feels different, like there's some exception that applies to me specifically that doesn't apply to anyone else. I know that sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but the feeling is still there.
therapist: You just caught something really important — you're holding yourself to a completely different standard than you'd apply to anyone else, and you can even hear how unfair that is when you say it out loud. That "exception that applies to me specifically" is worth exploring, because it didn't appear from nowhere — often it's rooted in an older, deeper belief about ourselves that predates the job. Where do you think that sense of being the exception might originally come from?

client: That's a hard question to sit with, because I think it probably goes back to growing up with parents who had really high expectations and where mistakes were kind of treated like a big deal. I always felt like I had to prove myself constantly, and even when I did well it was more like "okay, but what's next" rather than anyone really acknowledging it. I guess I never really learned how to let success stick, if that makes sense.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage to look at, and it makes so much sense — when success was never allowed to land or be celebrated growing up, your brain never got to build that internal foundation of "I am capable." The good news is that what was learned in that environment can, with time, be gently relearned. I'm curious, what do you think it would feel like to actually let a success — like that spring campaign — fully count for you, even just for a moment?

client: Honestly, just trying to imagine that right now feels kind of uncomfortable, like there's almost a superstition around it — as if letting myself feel good about something means I'm setting myself up to fail the next time. I think it would feel relieving for a second, but then immediately scary, like the ground might disappear underneath me. I'm not sure I even know how to do that without it feeling forced or fake.
therapist: That "superstition" you're describing is such a honest and insightful way to name it — it's like your nervous system learned that feeling good is dangerous, that it lets your guard down right before something goes wrong. That belief was probably protective once, in an environment where the next expectation was always around the corner, but it's costing you a lot now. I'm wondering, is there a very small, low-stakes success from recently — even something tiny — where you might experiment with letting it count, just briefly, without it needing to feel completely natural yet?

client: There was actually a moment earlier this week where I put together a client presentation pretty quickly and my manager mentioned it looked polished, which I kind of just brushed off in the moment. I could try to let that one count, but I'm already feeling this urge to qualify it — like "yeah but it was a short presentation, it wasn't that big a deal." I guess I'm not sure how to just sit with it without my brain immediately finding a reason to shrink it down.
therapist: It's really telling that the qualifying thought arrived almost instantly — your brain is so practiced at shrinking these moments that it happens almost automatically, like a reflex. But notice what's actually true: you produced something polished, quickly, and someone whose opinion matters confirmed it — that's real, and the presentation's length doesn't cancel that out. What if, just for this week, you tried treating that compliment like a small deposit into an internal account — not a big dramatic shift, just letting it sit there without immediately withdrawing it?

client: I like the idea of a deposit, that framing actually makes it feel a little less overwhelming than telling myself to "believe in myself" or something big like that. But I'm honestly not sure what that looks like practically — like, do I just remind myself of it when the anxiety spikes, or is there something more concrete I'm supposed to do? I'm a little worried that without some kind of structure I'll just forget about it the moment I'm back under the pressure of those two new projects.
therapist: It's great that the deposit framing resonates — and your instinct to want something concrete is really wise, because vague intentions tend to dissolve under pressure. One practical approach would be keeping a small running note on your phone — even just a sentence or two — where you briefly log moments like the presentation compliment as they happen, so when anxiety spikes around these new projects you have something tangible to actually look at rather than trying to summon the memory from scratch. Would something like that feel manageable to try this week, or is there a different format that might fit better into how you already move through your day?

client: A note on my phone feels doable, but I'm already thinking about how when I'm in the thick of a stressful workday I barely have time to eat lunch, let alone stop and write something down. I guess my worry is that I'll set this up with good intentions and then feel guilty when I inevitably forget to log things, which would just become another thing I'm failing at. Is there a way to make it even simpler, like maybe just a one-word log or something that takes literally ten seconds?
therapist: A one-word log is a genuinely great idea — even just typing "presentation" or "polished" takes seconds and still makes that deposit real and retrievable. And I want to gently point out something you just did: you anticipated a perfectly reasonable adaptation and immediately framed it as future failure, which is that same protective reflex we've been talking about all session. What if the rule was simply that *any* entry counts, even a single word once a week, so there's no version of this where you're failing at it?
